_comment: Copy this to a study config and fill in the placeholders. GENERATED from SPEC in scripts/ls_config.py by `python scripts/ls_config.py --write-example` - edit the spec, not this file.
source_dir: <ABSOLUTE PATH TO THE FOLDER OF .czi FILES>
_atlas_pdf_note: Only 04a, 04a2 and 04a4 open it, to extract plates again. The extracted plates themselves ship in atlas/ and are copied into <out_root>/atlas/ the first time a study needs them.
atlas_pdf: <ABSOLUTE PATH TO THE ATLAS PDF, OR EMPTY>
_export_dir_note: One folder per export, named DD.MM.YYYY_HH.MM, with the same stamp on every file in it. Read by 04l (shown in the page, and the default for --export-dir) and by the app's download handler, so the two cannot disagree. A browser writes here only after the operator picks the folder with the page's Folder... button - a web page cannot be handed a path.
export_dir: <ABSOLUTE PATH FOR CURATOR EXPORTS, OR EMPTY>

slide_naming._pattern_note: Built by the app's pattern builder, and editable by hand. A filename that does not match is REPORTED, never silently skipped - an invisible file is the failure mode this whole block exists to prevent. `subject` becomes the `animal` column and the first field of every scene_uid, so it is the key the metadata join later runs on.

_section_order_convention_note: Confirmed by user 2026-08-11 for the LS dataset. Serial order = scene index as acquired. The scanner ran column-major (s0 top-left, s1 below it, s2 next column top), and on staggered slides such as LS120_1a no grid model reproduces the physical layout at all.
_pixel_size_um_note: The CZI carries this too - czi_meta.py reads it from Scaling/Items/Distance[@Id='X'] - so a future revision should check this value against the files rather than trust it.
_section_thickness_um_note: NOT recoverable from the CZIs - they carry no size_z, being single-plane images of a physical section - so it has to be supplied. This is the number the Abercrombie correction needs; see detection.abercrombie below. 14.0 for the LS dataset, operator-stated 2026-08-30.

curation_render._source_note: `czi` renders each composite from the CZI's own 16-bit pixels in ONE resampling, onto the same frame the landmarks are stored in. `overview` is the old route: the 8-bit 5.2 um/px overview, squashed square and resampled three times, which shows about 8 um per screen pixel. Existing composites are kept until 04o runs with --force.
curation_render._um_per_px_note: 1.3 at the finest. The CZI is 0.65 um/px, but a whole section at that resolution is one picture of 10,000+ px a side - several GB to render and more than a browser holds comfortably - so 04o refuses anything finer than 1.3. 2.6 is already twice as sharp per pixel as the overview route, and the curator's zoom shows every pixel of it. Measurement (05c) always reads native pixels, whatever this says.

scene_render._out_dir_note: 01l writes <folder>/<marker>/stain+DAPI/ and <folder>/<marker>/stain_only/ here, one PNG per scene. Any folder will do, including one outside the study: nothing downstream reads these pictures. The table saying how each was drawn always stays at <out_root>/qc/scene_renders.csv, so the app can tell the step has run wherever the pictures went.
scene_render.out_dir: <ABSOLUTE PATH FOR SCENE PICTURES, OR EMPTY>
scene_render._um_per_px_note: 0.65 is the scan's own pixels, the finest there is; larger numbers give smaller, softer pictures (5.2 is the overviews' scale). Each picture pixel is the average of whole native 0.65 um pixels, so the value is rounded to a multiple of 0.65 and the table records what was drawn. Memory: a whole scene at 0.65 can need several GB. Each scene is checked against the memory (RAM plus page file) free at the time, and one that does not fit is skipped with a message rather than crashing the run; 1.3 needs a quarter of that, 2.6 a sixteenth.
scene_render._source_note: `scan` (the default) averages the scan's own 0.65 um pixels into each picture pixel, here. `zeiss_preview` instead loads the smaller copy of each scan that the Zeiss software stored inside the CZI when the slide was scanned: about ten times faster (15 of every 16 pixels are never unpacked), same resolution, but Zeiss did the averaging and compressed that copy separately, so pixel values differ slightly from `scan` and the edges of saturated (clipped) patches can look a little softer. Only the scene pictures change. Nothing is measured from them: detection and counting (05c), clipping masks, the overviews and the curator pictures always read the scan's own pixels, whatever this says. Fastest at 1.3, 2.6 or 5.2 um/px, where Zeiss stored a copy; at 0.65 both choices read the scan itself. Changing it redraws the pictures on the next run.
scene_render._range_note: `dataset` uses the overviews' frozen range (qc/display_ranges.json), so the same brightness means the same signal in every picture; the brightest nuclei can saturate at fine resolutions. `section` stretches each scene to its own tissue: every picture well exposed, but brightness no longer compares between pictures. A frozen range pushed to the top by clipped pixels is stretched per scene in either mode.

curation_coverage._sections_per_level_note: A goal to curate towards, nothing more: no stage reads it, and nothing is held or refused below it. The levels counted are the plates curated sections were placed on in the newest ROI export, so a level no animal has reached yet is not listed. 1 asks for every animal to be represented at every level any animal was curated at, which is what a matched-level comparison needs.

acquisition._layout_note: `multiplex` is one scan per section carrying every marker as a channel, which is what a new study should be. `paired` is the LS layout: each marker is a separate physical scan of the same section, joined by 02_pair_passes. Paired declares no channel table, because each of its scans carries the nuclear channel plus whichever marker that pass used.
acquisition._channels_note: One entry per channel: `name` is the identity used in every output path and the `marker` column; `role` is nuclear, marker, registration or ignore; `czi_name` is what the microscope calls it, which is how it is located in a file; `index` is the plane to fall back on. A marker also carries `segment` (nuclear or own), and for own, a `backend` and whether its objects are `nucleus_shaped`. Empty for the paired layout.
acquisition._markers_note: A paired study declares no channel table, because each of its scans carries the nuclear channel plus whichever marker that pass used - so this list is the only record of what the markers are. It is NOT derived from the manifest's marker_channel column: every constant built from it is evaluated at import, and the manifest lives under out_root, which may be absent. Output paths, CSV column values and workbook sheets are built from these names, so changing one renames real files.
acquisition._marker_segmentation_note: A paired study declares no channel table, so every marker takes the nuclear route: StarDist on the counterstain, the marker measured inside the mask. That is wrong for a pass whose counterstain plane is unusable. The LS PCNA (AF488) scans carry a DAPI plane that is noise at native resolution, so there is nothing to segment. Declaring `{"AF488": {"segment": "own", "backend": "stardist", "nucleus_shaped": true}}` segments PCNA on its own channel. Use it only for a marker whose signal is nuclear (PCNA is): StarDist is a nucleus detector. The cost is real and 06a records it: with no counterstain there is no count of all cells, so the fraction positive and the total cell density are withheld for that marker and the readout is positive density. See docs/nuclei-detection-after-roi-curation.md section 4.8.

display._composite_note: Empty means every declared marker, in declared order. This order is what the positional colour default reads - the first marker listed here is red, the second green - so a study can swap two markers' colours either by reordering this or by naming the colours in `display.colours`. A marker left out of a non-empty list is still measured; it is simply not drawn, which is visible rather than silently blended into another marker's colour.
display._colours_note: Empty means positional: the first marker shown is red, the second green, and any marker beyond the second HAS NO COLOUR. A marker with no colour is measured but NOT DRAWN - absent from the section composites, which say so and stop rather than building them, and grey in the curator's Review pane, which labels it "no colour set". Both say so rather than picking one, because a marker silently wearing another marker's colour is exactly the fault this key was added to remove: the Review pane used to draw every marker but one in green while the composites beside it drew the first in red. Names: blue, cyan, green, grey, magenta, orange, red, white, yellow. Anything else must be six hex digits.
display._nuclear_colour_note: Blue is what every composite and every curator page this pipeline has produced has used, and the geometry channel is the counterstain - so the blue plane of a composite is the byte-for-byte greyscale the landmarks were placed on, and `04o --verify` checks exactly that. Changing this changes what --verify is comparing. Where a marker shares a plane with the counterstain - a magenta marker has blue in it - the two are combined with max rather than added, so neither is clipped.

channels._dapi_index_note: Read only by 05c_detect_rois today; every earlier stage assumes plane 0 structurally. The channels/markers sub-project replaces this whole block with a per-channel role table, so it is left as-is rather than changed twice.

_marker_identity_note: Fluorophore -> marker name, e.g. {"AF568": "pERK"}. Written by 00c --accept and read by no stage. Until it is filled in, no fluorophore may be referred to by a biological name downstream. For the nuclear counterstain, record excitation and emission in nm by reading them off the CZI channel metadata (ExcitationWavelength / EmissionWavelength, exposed by scripts/czi_meta.py) rather than quoting a datasheet - what matters is the filter set actually used, not the dye in the abstract. Kept because it is the only written record of the confirmed assignment; the channels/markers sub-project wires it.

abercrombie._enabled_note: A single-plane image of a section counts nuclear PROFILES, not nuclei: a nucleus straddling the cut face still appears in the section it is cut into. Abercrombie N = n * T/(T + h), with T the section thickness and h the mean diameter of the counted object along the axis perpendicular to the section. At T=14 and h=7 the factor is 0.667 - uncorrected counts are 50% too high. h is MEASURED per marker and region from the nuclear-counterstain segmentation, not taken from nucleus_diameter_um above: that value is a detection-scale assumption, and the factor moves from 0.737 to 0.583 across a plausible 5-10 um range, so using it would bury an unmeasured constant in every density. Abercrombie assumes spherical, randomly positioned objects and applies no lost-caps correction; the unbiased alternative is the optical or physical disector, which needs z-stacks a single-plane dataset does not have. Report raw and corrected counts side by side and say which is which. This is also why it is enabled rather than optional: where sections are cut consecutively, adjacent sections are not independent tissue - a nucleus cut by the boundary appears in both - so summing or averaging raw profile counts across neighbours double-counts it.

threshold._mad_k_note: 3.0 is the same multiplier 06a uses for the positivity cut, so the pipeline has one definition of `above background` rather than two. Raising it finds fewer, brighter objects. It is applied to the frame being segmented rather than to curated background discs, because 05c runs before 06a and cannot read a file 06a has not written. Median and MAD rather than mean and SD because the objects are in the sample: a bright object would raise the very cut meant to find it.
threshold._min_area_um2_note: Not tidying. At k=3 over a whole frame, thousands of single-pixel excursions clear the cut by chance and each one would be counted as an object. This is what makes the count mean `a stained region` rather than `a pixel that was noisy`. 5 um2 is well below a nucleus (a 7 um nucleus is ~38 um2) and well above sensor noise; a study counting something smaller must lower it deliberately.

stardist._prob_thresh_note: Setting it here overrides the tuned value. Lower finds more, dimmer objects and more noise; higher finds fewer. Changing it after detection has started changes what a nucleus is, so 05c refuses to add sections measured with a different value to the ones already measured: re-run detection with Redo finished sections.
stardist._nms_thresh_note: Not tuned by 05b: the model was trained with its own value, and nothing measured on the slides says it should move. Raise it only if touching nuclei are being merged in the QC pictures.
stardist._use_auto_note: Off runs detection with the model's own thresholds (or the ones set above), which is what every count before 05b existed was made with. The measurements and the tuned values stay in detection.auto either way.

_atlas_source_note: salmon takes its plates from atlas_pdf and atlas_plate_set. wullimann1996 is the zebrafish cross-section atlas: 04w builds its plate set (plates_wullimann), 04x turns each plate's region outlines into numbered polygons, and atlas_plate_set is then ignored. Plate ids differ between the two (wplate_NNN), and the plate fingerprint the importers already check catches rows made against another plate set. An atlas made elsewhere is brought in with `python scripts/ls_atlas_import.py` or the Import atlas button, which registers it under `atlases` and is then a valid value here.
_atlas_rebuild_plates_note: The salmon and Wullimann plates ship ready-made in the repository's atlas/ folder and are copied into <out_root>/atlas/ when a study first needs them, so the extraction stages (04a-04a4, 04w, 04x) are not part of a study that uses them. Turn this on only to remake a plate set from the PDF - for example plates_merged, which does not ship. Plates made again are different pictures: sections curated against the shipped ones then read as changed.
_atlas_polygon_mirror_note: Each Wullimann plate draws one hemisphere beside the micrograph of the other, so the outlines cover half the brain. Mirroring gives the numbered guide on both sides in 04l. Registration (04e) always mirrors, because it reads the micrograph half.
_atlases_note: Written by `python scripts/ls_atlas_import.py` (or the app's Import atlas button), not by hand. Each entry names a plate set under <out_root>/atlas/ - its own folder, never one a built-in uses - and says how its regions are marked (`region_kind`: seeds or polygons), whether each plate carries a micrograph half (`micrograph_half`) and whether its polygons can be mirrored (`mirror_allowed`). `atlas_source` then accepts the entry's name. An entry is judged strictly when read: a bad one is an error, not a quiet fall back to salmon.

atlas_plate_set._dir_note: Both read this, so they cannot drift apart. IDs COLLIDE between sets - the same plate_NNN name exists in more than one set and points at a different image - so a landmark file records the set it was made against. Set this once, before any landmark is placed; changing it later invalidates landmarks made against the old set. plates_final = one section per plate, cut from the salmon atlas and curated (64 plates) - use this one. plates = the pictures as extracted from the PDF, one per page: from page 15 on each holds TWO sections stacked, so the ROI curator and registration would treat two brain levels as one plate. plates_merged = one image per figure, an intermediate step.

atlas_figure_sections._two_sections_note: Operator knowledge, not measurement: the band detector in 04a2 mis-counts when two sections touch (their legend text bridges every row, so no row is empty) and when one section is crossed by an internal white band (read as two). This declaration is the authority; the detector is not. 04a3b_enforce_sections.py takes the count from here and decides only WHERE to cut. Record the date and the reason alongside it when you fill it in.
atlas_figure_sections._drop_inset_boxes_note: Boxes that are labelled INSETS, not sections - a detached callout of a structure that is also shown attached and labelled inside a section elsewhere in the atlas. An inset is not a plate, and holds no region seed. Empty by default on purpose: an entry is a claim about a figure in YOUR atlas, and a copied one would drop a real section box. Note that listing a figure here also exempts it from the two_sections count above, so list only the figures that really carry an inset.

_atlas_scope_note: Names are matched EXACTLY as the atlas writes them - no abbreviating, no reinterpreting - so the anatomy stays the atlas author's statement rather than this file's. In the ROI curator, `existing_regions` is the pre-ticked list (in that order) the first time the 'Which ROIs will you draw?' window opens; one that no plate of the atlas carries is flagged, since it is a typo or the wrong atlas. `regions_to_add` are regions you want that this atlas does not have: they are listed, greyed, under 'not in this atlas' so the gap is visible instead of silent. `mode` is a recorded label only.

groups._order_note: Explicit because dict order is not a decision. Two entries: the slide splits in two.
groups._by_animal_note: UNBLINDING KEY. A DELIBERATE EXCEPTION to the blinding rule ('no stage before 06b may read a group label'): a figure that compares groups cannot be built without knowing them. Nothing here reaches a count, a threshold or a curation decision - the curator's own state is written before this file is read and does not depend on it - but a deck laid out by group is, by construction, not blind. Leave empty to keep it that way; the Shotgun button disables itself when it is. An animal left out is reported and skipped rather than guessed at. The metadata-join sub-project replaces this with a real table join.
